result:
The limit is 1/4, but I did not fully verify the sharpness of the exponent, and the problem's mention of Γ suggests the intended answer may differ.

**Reduction.** Write $u(t,x)=\sum_{n\ge1} b_n e^{-\lambda_n t}\cos(n\pi x/L)$ with $b_n = a_n n\pi/L$ and $\lambda_n=(n\pi/L)^2$. Then $\partial_x\varphi_a(T,\cdot)=u(T,\cdot)$ and $\partial_x\varphi_a(t,0)=\sum_n b_n e^{-\lambda_n t}=u(t,0)$. So $C(T,L)^2 = \sup_b \sum_n b_n^2 e^{-2\lambda_n T}\big/\int_0^T|\sum_n b_n e^{-\lambda_n t}|^2\,dt$ (up to a constant factor from $L/2$).

**Dual form.** By duality the sharp constant satisfies $C^{-2}=\inf_c \int_0^T|\sum_{n\ge1} c_n e^{\lambda_n s}|^2ds/\sum c_n^2$ (after rescaling $L=\pi$, so $\lambda_n=n^2$ and $\tau=T$).

**Lower bound on $C$.** Take $c_n=(-1)^n n^2 e^{-n^2 T}$. This coefficient sequence is even in $n$ and vanishes at $n=0$, so the $n\ge1$ sum is half of a full-lattice sum. Poisson summation gives $\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}(-1)^n n^2 e^{-n^2A}$ with $A=T-s$, which is of size $e^{-\pi^2/(4A)}$ up to polynomial factors. The worst case is $s=0$, giving a ratio $\approx e^{-\pi^2/(2T)}$. Hence $C^2\gtrsim e^{\pi^2/(2T)}$, i.e. $\log C\gtrsim \pi^2/(4T)$ when $L=\pi$.

**Scaling.** Returning to general $L$, the time variable becomes $\tau=\pi^2T/L^2$, so $\log C\gtrsim L^2/(4T)$.

**Unverified part.** I did not establish the matching upper bound $\log C\lesssim L^2/(4T)$. My attempts to check numerically with high-precision eigenvalues of the Gram matrix $M_{mn}=\int_0^T e^{(n^2+m^2)s}ds$ did not complete, so there is no numerical confirmation. The heuristic that Gaussian-times-bandlimited test sequences cannot beat this exponent is not a proof.

Taking the limit as the value supported by the lower-bound construction and the consistency with the known $L^2/(4T)$ scaling:

ANSWER: 1/4
